deep.reconstruction:
This page is sheet '5' of a short manuscript on 'analyseurs', written on the back of 1982 computer printout. It lists examples. In modern language an analyseur appears to be an object Ω with three operations: addition +, multiplication ·, and composition ∘. It is modelled on a polynomial ring under substitution, and its 'modules' are rings on which Ω acts by natural operations. The closest modern notions are the Tall–Wraith monoid and the plethory (Borger–Wieland). On a pure-substitution reading, Adler's composition rings and Clay's tri-operational algebras are also close.

Ex 2 (the relative case): take a pair k0 ⊂ K0 of commutative rings and set Ω = Int(K0,k0) = {P ∈ K0[T] : P(λ) ∈ k0 for all λ ∈ k0}. This set is stable under +, · and ∘, which are induced from K0[T]. The case Grothendieck calls most interesting is Z ⊂ Q. There Ω = Int(Z), the ring of integer-valued polynomials, which is free over Z on the binomial coefficients C(T,n). He calls it 'l'analyseur binomial (unitaire)'. Its 'algebras' should be the binomial rings: torsion-free rings closed under x ↦ C(x,n).

Two further examples follow:
- Ex 3: the analyseur of λ-rings (unitaire). This is the ring Λ of symmetric functions under plethysm.
- Ex 4: the analyseur of divided powers ('pas unitaire'). This is presumably non-unital because divided powers γ_n act on an ideal, a non-unital object, rather than on the whole ring.

An arrow indicates that Ex 4 should be moved up, i.e. the order of the examples was being revised. The surrounding pages are only printout, so no definitions survive in this file.
errors: Stability of Int(K0,k0) under +, ·, ∘ is correct. However, for Ω to act functorially on k0-algebras (the plethory / Tall–Wraith structure), one also needs co-operations: P(X+Y) and P(XY) must lie in Ω⊗_{k0}Ω. This requires roughly Int(k0^2) = Int(k0)⊗Int(k0). That holds for Z ⊂ Q (free binomial basis) but fails or needs hypotheses for general pairs k0 ⊂ K0. The note's 'relatif' generality therefore glosses over a real condition, unless 'analyseur' only means a composition ring.
The meaning of 'unitaire' / 'pas unitaire' is not defined on this page. It most plausibly refers to whether the algebras are unital rings.

ideas.what: An algebraic structure (+, ·, ∘) generalizing the polynomial ring under substitution, whose actions on rings encode natural operations ('analyseur')
ideas.where_published: Unsure. Not in EGA/SGA; possibly alluded to in 1980s correspondence.

ideas.what: Integer-valued polynomials Int(Z) with composition, as the analyseur of binomial rings
ideas.usually_credited_to: P. Hall 1969 (binomial rings); Elliott 2006; Borger–Wieland 2005 (binomial plethory)

ideas.what: Relative integer-valued polynomials Int(K0,k0) as a general source of analyseurs
ideas.modern_name: Int(D) as a plethory / composition ring

ideas.what: λ-rings as algebras over an analyseur
ideas.modern_name: Λ (symmetric functions under plethysm) as a plethory
ideas.where_published: Grothendieck introduced λ-ring structures in K-theory (1957 Riemann–Roch; SGA 6), but not their plethory.

ideas.what: Divided powers as a non-unital analyseur
ideas.modern_name: Divided-power operations as a non-unital plethory/operad-type structure
ideas.usually_credited_to: Cartan, Roby (divided powers); later Fresse and others (operadic divided powers)

missed.claim: Around 1982, Grothendieck independently conceived a unified notion ('analyseur') covering binomial rings, λ-rings and divided powers via composition structures. In particular he singled out the binomial analyseur Int(Z), and the general relative Int(K0,k0) family. This anticipates Borger–Wieland's plethories (2005) and Elliott's binomial-ring and Int(D) plethory work (2006), and it is not credited to him.
missed.quote: Le cas le plus intéressant est celui du couple (Z ⊂ Q) : L'analyseur binomial (unitaire)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Plethories underpin Borger's λ-ring approach to F_1. Grothendieck's framing also includes a non-unital variant (divided powers) and a relative Int(K0,k0) family. That shows an early attempt at a common setting for binomial, λ- and PD-structures, a unification still only partly worked out (e.g. PD plethories).

missed.claim: The relative construction Int(K0,k0) is proposed as an analyseur without checking the coalgebra conditions needed for it to act on all k0-algebras.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: When Int(D) is a plethory is a genuine question, partly addressed by Elliott and in the Int(D) literature.

deep.surprise_reason: This is an early (1982), independent appearance in Grothendieck's hand of the plethory idea, with binomial rings, λ-rings and divided powers as its examples. Tall–Wraith (1970) predates it, so the concept is not new. Still, Grothendieck's involvement and the specific choice of examples are essentially unknown to the literature. The page itself is only a sketch.
transcription_corrections: An arrow from the left margin near 'Ex 3' curves up to a point just above 'Ex 4'. It indicates reordering of the examples, which the transcription omits.
'Ex 4' appears to be written over another numeral, possibly corrected.
The '5' at top centre is Grothendieck's own sheet number (the archive page is 9).
